title: Cupido Ascanius. Convivium Didonis
titleEn: Cupid in Ascanius's Shape; Dido's Banquet — Aeneid I.657–756
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Venus, uneasy about the double-tongued Tyrians and about Juno, whose anger still burns, plots a new stratagem: Cupid is to take the face of dear Ascanius and set the queen on fire with the gifts. She asks her son, the only source of her strength, who scorns even the thunderbolts of the king of the gods, for his help. Aeneas, his brother, is tossed round every shore by Juno's hatred, as he well knows. Dido is holding Aeneas with kind words, and Venus fears where Juno's hospitality may lead; so she means to catch the queen with guile and ring her with flame before any god can change her, and to bind her to Aeneas by great love. Her plan is this. The boy is about to go to the city with gifts at his father's summons; she will lay him asleep on high Cythera or at Idalium, so that he cannot know of the trick or break in on it. Cupid is to wear the boy's looks for a single night, so that when Dido takes him in her lap at the royal feast, among the wine, and gives him embraces and kisses, he may breathe a hidden fire into her and deceive her with poison. Cupid obeys, lays his wings aside and walks off with Iulus's gait, while Venus pours calm sleep through Ascanius's limbs and carries him to the Idalian groves, where soft marjoram wraps him in flowers and fragrant shade. Cupid arrives with the Tyrians' royal gifts, Achates leading. The queen is already enthroned on a golden couch amid proud hangings; Aeneas and the Trojans come, and all sit on purple. Servants bring water for the hands, bread in baskets and towels of shorn wool; fifty maids set out the long store of food and tend the hearth gods with fire, a hundred more maids and as many men of like age load the tables and set out cups; Tyrians throng in and recline on painted couches. All marvel at the gifts, at Iulus and at the glowing face and feigned words of the god (a bracketed line, 711, which Greenough marks as spurious, adds the robe and the embroidered veil). Above all the unlucky Dido, doomed to ruin to come, cannot take her fill, and burns with gazing, moved alike by boy and gifts. When he has hung on Aeneas's neck and satisfied the love of his false father, he goes to the queen; she clings to him with eyes and whole heart, and sometimes warms him in her lap, never knowing how great a god is settling on her. He, remembering his Acidalian mother, begins little by little to wipe out Sychaeus and to catch with a living love a heart long idle. When the first pause comes in the feast and the tables are cleared, they set up great mixing bowls and wreathe the wine; noise fills the halls and lamps hang burning from the golden ceiling. Dido calls for the heavy jewelled cup that Belus and his line had used, fills it with wine, and, in silence, prays: may Jupiter, giver of the laws of hospitality, make this a happy day for Tyrians and Trojans and for their descendants; may Bacchus and kindly Juno be present; and she bids the Tyrians keep the feast with good omen. She pours a libation, touches the cup to her lips, hands it to Bitias, who drains it eagerly, and other nobles follow. Long-haired Iopas, taught by great Atlas, makes his gilded lyre ring: he sings the wandering moon and the toils of the sun, the beginning of men and beasts, rain and fire, Arcturus, the rainy Hyades and the twin Bears, and why the winter suns hurry to dip in Ocean and what holds back the slow nights. The Tyrians applaud and the Trojans follow. Ill-fated Dido spins out the night in talk and takes in love with every word, asking much of Priam and Hector, of the arms Memnon wore, of Diomedes's horses, of how great Achilles was. At last she asks Aeneas to tell, from the first beginning, the Greeks' treachery, the fortunes of his people and his own wanderings, for the seventh summer already carries him over every land and sea.
part: Cupid in Ascanius's Shape; Dido's Banquet (I.657–756)

sentences.t:
At Cytherea novas artes, nova pectore versat
Consilia, ut faciem mutatus et ora Cupido
pro dulci Ascanio veniat, donisque furentem
incendat reginam, atque ossibus implicet ignem;
sentences.l:
But Cytherea turns over new arts, new plans in her breast,
that Cupid, changed in face and features, may come
in place of sweet Ascanius, and with the gifts may set the frenzied
queen on fire, and twine the flame about her bones;
sentences.i: But Cytherea turns over in her heart new devices and new schemes: Cupid is to come in the changed face and features of dear Ascanius, and with the gifts set the distracted queen ablaze and wind the fire into her very bones;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Cytherea' is Venus, named from the island of Cythera, near which she was said to have come ashore. 'At' marks the turn from Aeneas's party to Venus's worry. 'novas artes, nova… consilia' — the two objects of 'versat' ('turns over', i.e. ponders), with the repeated 'nova' for emphasis. 'ut… veniat… incendat… implicet' — purpose clauses (ut + present subjunctive) spelling out the 'consilia'. 'faciem mutatus et ora' — 'changed as to face and features': a passive participle with accusative of respect, a Greek-style construction you will see constantly. 'pro dulci Ascanio' — 'in place of' him. 'donis' — the gifts Aeneas has sent for (the robe, veil, sceptre and necklace of 647–655). 'furentem' — 'raving', 'frenzied', foreshadowing the fury of love.

sentences.t: quippe domum timet ambiguam Tyriosque bilinguis;
sentences.l: for she fears the doubtful house and the double-tongued Tyrians;
sentences.i: for she fears the untrustworthy palace and the double-tongued Tyrians;
sentences.n: 'quippe' — 'for indeed' (giving the reason). 'domum ambiguam' — the 'house' is the royal household (Dido's palace and court), 'doubtful' in loyalty. 'bilinguis' — accusative plural in -is (Greenough's spelling, as in 'montis', 'omnis') for the ordinary -es: 'two-tongued', i.e. treacherous. The Romans said the Carthaginians were faithless ('Punica fides'); Venus is already speaking as a Roman would.

sentences.t: urit atrox Iuno, et sub noctem cura recursat.
sentences.l: fierce Juno burns her, and with night's approach the care comes running back.
sentences.i: Fierce Juno torments her, and as night comes on, the worry returns.
sentences.n: 'urit' — 'burns', 'torments', with the object ('her', Venus) left out; the verb of burning is the first hint of the fire motif of the whole scene. 'atrox' — 'savage', 'harsh'. 'recursat' — a frequentative verb (recurrit, 'keeps running back'): the worry comes round again each evening.

sentences.t: Ergo his aligerum dictis adfatur Amorem:
sentences.l: So with these words she addresses winged Love:
sentences.i: So she speaks to winged Love in these words:
sentences.n: 'Ergo' — 'so', 'therefore'. 'his… dictis' — ablative of means. 'adfatur' — present of the deponent 'adfor' ('speaks to'), the narrative present of the scene, with the colon leading into the speech. 'aligerum' — accusative singular of 'aliger', 'wing-bearing', agreeing with 'Amorem'. 'Amor' is Cupid; both names are used in this part.

sentences.t:
“Nate, meae vires, mea magna potentia solus,
nate, patris summi qui tela Typhoia temnis,
ad te confugio et supplex tua numina posco.
sentences.l:
“Son, my strength, you alone my great power,
son, who scorn the Typhoean weapons of the father most high,
to you I flee, and as a suppliant ask your divine power.
sentences.i: “My son, my strength, my one great power, my son, who make light of the Typhoean bolts of the father on high: to you I flee, and as a suppliant I implore your godhead.
sentences.n: Venus's speech to Cupid (664–688); the mark opens it. The opening is full of vocatives: 'nate' twice, then 'meae vires' and 'mea magna potentia', stacked in apposition, with 'solus' ('you alone') agreeing with the 'you' of the address. 'patris summi' — 'of the father on high', Jupiter; the phrase does not say that Cupid is his son (the stories about Cupid's father differ), only that Cupid scorns Jupiter's weapons. 'Typhoia' — Greek-form adjective: Typhoeus (Typhon) was the monster Jupiter struck down with thunderbolts and buried under Etna; 'tela Typhoia' are those same bolts, which Cupid, whose arrows reach even Jupiter, 'despises'. 'temnis' — 'qui temnis', relative clause, 'you who scorn'. 'ad te confugio' — the language of prayer; 'supplex' and 'numina' make Venus a petitioner of her own son. 'posco' — 'ask for', 'beg'.

sentences.t:
Frater ut Aeneas pelago tuus omnia circum
litora iactetur odiis Iunonis iniquae,
nota tibi, et nostro doluisti saepe dolore.
sentences.l:
How your brother Aeneas, on the sea, round all
shores is tossed by the hatreds of unjust Juno
is known to you, and often you have grieved with our grief.
sentences.i: You know how your brother Aeneas is flung from shore to shore across the sea by the hatred of unfair Juno, and you have often shared my grief.
sentences.n: 'Frater… Aeneas' — Cupid and Aeneas are both sons of Venus (Aeneas by Anchises). 'ut… iactetur' — an indirect question with the subjunctive, 'how he is tossed', depending on 'nota (sunt)' — 'nota tibi' is a verbless 'it is known to you'. 'omnia circum litora' — 'circum' placed after its noun (anastrophe), 'round all shores'. 'odiis' — ablative of cause or means, plural for the hatred as it keeps showing itself. 'iniquae' — 'unjust', 'unfair'. 'nostro… dolore' — 'with our grief': Venus's plural for singular, with the ablative of cause after 'doluisti'.

sentences.t:
Hunc Phoenissa tenet Dido blandisque moratur
vocibus;
sentences.l:
Him Phoenician Dido holds and delays with kind
words;
sentences.i: The Phoenician Dido is keeping him with her, and detains him with kind words;
sentences.n: 'Phoenissa… Dido' — Dido is from Tyre in Phoenicia. 'tenet' — 'holds', 'keeps'; 'moratur' — 'delays', 'keeps waiting' (both mean he cannot leave). 'blandis… vocibus' — the adjective 'blandus' means 'flattering', 'caressing'; the noun 'vocibus' is carried over to the start of the next line (enjambment).

sentences.t:
et vereor, quo se Iunonia vertant
hospitia;
sentences.l:
and I fear whither Juno's welcome
may turn;
sentences.i: and I fear where Juno's welcome may lead;
sentences.n: 'vereor, quo se… vertant' — an indirect question with the subjunctive, 'I fear whither they may turn themselves'. 'Iunonia hospitia' — 'Juno's hospitality', the plural of 'hospitium' ('welcome', 'entertainment') with the adjective 'Iunonia' ('of Juno'): Venus suspects that Dido's friendly welcome of the Trojans has Juno behind it, and does not trust Juno's motive. Carthage is Juno's favourite city (15–18).

sentences.t: haud tanto cessabit cardine rerum.
sentences.l: she will not be idle at so great a hinge of affairs.
sentences.i: she will not stand idle at so critical a turning point.
sentences.n: The subject (Juno) is understood. 'cardine rerum' — 'hinge of affairs': a hinge is the pivot a door turns on, so 'cardo' is a point at which things turn. 'haud' negates 'cessabit' ('will hang back', 'be inactive'), a future tense; 'tanto' agrees with 'cardine', an ablative of circumstance ('at so great a hinge').

sentences.t:
Quocirca capere ante dolis et cingere flamma
reginam meditor, ne quo se numine mutet,
sed magno Aeneae mecum teneatur amore.
sentences.l:
Therefore beforehand I plan to catch by guile and to girdle with flame
the queen, lest by some divinity she change herself,
but be held with me by a great love for Aeneas.
sentences.i: So I mean to trap the queen beforehand by guile and to ring her round with flame, so that no god's influence may change her, but she may be held fast, with me, by a great love of Aeneas.
sentences.n: 'Quocirca' — 'wherefore'. 'meditor' — 'I plan', with the infinitives 'capere' and 'cingere'. 'ante' — 'beforehand', before Juno can act. 'dolis' — ablative of means. 'flamma' — the fire of love. 'ne quo… numine mutet' — 'ne quo' = 'ne aliquo' ('lest by any'); 'se mutet' — 'change herself', i.e. change her attitude to the Trojans (Juno's influence). 'sed… teneatur' — the contrasting subjunctive (still a 'ne… sed' purpose clause). 'mecum' — 'together with me', i.e. as an ally of Venus. 'Aeneae amore' — 'love for Aeneas': a genitive of the object.

sentences.t: Qua facere id possis, nostram nunc accipe mentem.
sentences.l: By what means you may do this, now take our plan.
sentences.i: Now hear my plan for how you may do it.
sentences.n: 'Qua facere id possis' — an indirect question depending on 'accipe mentem', with 'qua' an adverb ('by what way?'); 'possis' is a subjunctive in the indirect question. 'nostram… mentem' — 'our' for 'my', the common plural of the speaker. 'mentem' — 'intention', 'plan'.

sentences.t:
Regius accitu cari genitoris ad urbem
Sidoniam puer ire parat, mea maxima cura,
dona ferens, pelago et flammis restantia Troiae:
sentences.l:
The royal one, at the summons of his dear father, to the city
Sidonian the boy prepares to go, my greatest care,
bringing gifts that survived the sea and the flames of Troy:
sentences.i: The royal boy, my chief concern, is getting ready to go to the Sidonian city at his dear father's summons, bringing gifts saved from the sea and the flames of Troy:
sentences.n: 'Regius… puer' — Ascanius, the king's (Aeneas's) son, he was named at 659 ('dulci Ascanio'), and the speech does not name him again. 'accitu' — ablative of 'accitus', a noun used only in the ablative singular: 'at the summoning'. 'Sidoniam' — 'Sidonian' is used for 'Tyrian' or 'Phoenician' (Sidon was the other great Phoenician city), here an adjective with 'urbem' (Carthage). 'mea maxima cura' — nominative in apposition to 'puer'. 'restantia' — 'surviving', 'remaining'; it agrees with 'dona'. 'pelago et flammis' is most simply taken as datives (the gifts 'stood out against' sea and fire), though some take them as ablatives, 'left over from' them; either way the sense is that the gifts outlasted the sea and the burning of Troy.

sentences.t:
hunc ego sopitum somno super alta Cythera
aut super Idalium sacrata sede recondam,
ne qua scire dolos mediusve occurrere possit.
sentences.l:
him, I, lulled in sleep, over high Cythera
or over Idalium, in a holy dwelling, will hide,
lest in any way he be able to know the tricks or, coming between, to meet them.
sentences.i: I shall hide him, wrapped in sleep, on lofty Cythera or in my holy seat at Idalium, so that he can neither learn of the trick nor step in and spoil it.
sentences.n: 'hunc ego sopitum somno' — 'him, I, lulled by sleep' (perfect passive participle with an ablative of means). 'recondam' — future, 'I will put away'. Cythera and Idalium (Idalium is in Cyprus) were both centres of Venus's cult. 'super' — with the accusative, 'over', 'on top of', i.e. 'on' the high place. 'sacrata sede' — ablative of place; 'sedes' is a 'seat' (the sanctuary). 'ne qua… possit' — negative purpose; after 'ne', 'qua' is the adverb 'in any way' (the 'ali-' of 'aliqua' dropped, as in 'ne quo' above). 'mediusve occurrere' — 'mediusve' agrees with the subject: 'coming in the middle, in between'; 'occurrere' means 'meet' the plot, and 'dolos' is the object of both infinitives.

sentences.t:
Tu faciem illius noctem non amplius unam
falle dolo, et notos pueri puer indue voltus,
sentences.l:
You his appearance, for one night, not more than one,
deceive with guile, and, a boy, put on the boy's known features,
sentences.i: For one night, no more than one, counterfeit his looks, and, yourself a boy, take on the well-known features of the boy,
sentences.n: 'faciem illius' — the object of 'falle', whose usual object is the person deceived; here it is 'deceive his form with guile', i.e. 'counterfeit'. 'noctem… unam' — accusative of duration. 'notos pueri puer indue voltus' — the repeated 'puer', set side by side (boy putting on the boy's face), is a deliberate play. 'voltus' is Greenough's spelling of 'vultus'. 'indue' — imperative of 'induo', 'put on' (a garment).

sentences.t:
ut, cum te gremio accipiet laetissima Dido
regalis inter mensas laticemque Lyaeum,
cum dabit amplexus atque oscula dulcia figet,
occultum inspires ignem fallasque veneno.”
sentences.l:
that, when most happy Dido takes you in her lap
among the royal tables and the Lyaean liquor,
when she gives embraces and plants sweet kisses,
you may breathe in a hidden fire and deceive her with poison.”
sentences.i: so that when Dido, overjoyed, takes you on her lap amid the royal tables and the wine of Lyaeus, and gives you embraces and presses sweet kisses on you, you may breathe a secret fire into her and cheat her with poison.”
sentences.n: 'ut… inspires fallasque' — a purpose clause, two subjunctives, and the sentence is the sequel to the instruction in 683–684. 'cum… accipiet… cum dabit… figet' — 'cum' with the future indicative, 'when she will receive… will give… will plant'. 'laetissima' — superlative: 'most happy'. 'regalis' — accusative plural in -is (Greenough's spelling) for the ordinary -es. 'regalis inter mensas' — 'inter' after its noun (anastrophe). 'Lyaeum' — an epithet of Bacchus, 'Lyaeus', the Looser (from Greek 'lyein', to loosen: he looses care), so 'laticem Lyaeum' is 'the liquid of Lyaeus', i.e. wine. 'veneno' — 'poison', love's drug, with the same figure of fire and poison running together. The closing mark ends Venus's speech.

sentences.t:
Paret Amor dictis carae genetricis, et alas
exuit, et gressu gaudens incedit Iuli.
sentences.l:
Love obeys the words of his dear mother, and puts off his wings,
and walks, rejoicing in the gait of Iulus.
sentences.i: Love obeys his dear mother's words, takes off his wings, and walks along, glad, with the gait of Iulus.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'dictis' — dative with 'paret' ('obeys the words'). 'alas exuit' — 'takes off his wings' as one takes off clothing. 'gressu… Iuli' — ablative of respect, 'in the step of Iulus'. 'Iulus' is Ascanius's other name; by the poem's own account (267–288) it is the name from which the Julian family, including Caesar and Augustus, took theirs.

sentences.t:
At Venus Ascanio placidam per membra quietem
inrigat, et fotum gremio dea tollit in altos
Idaliae lucos, ubi mollis amaracus illum
floribus et dulci adspirans complectitur umbra.
sentences.l:
But Venus pours calm rest through Ascanius's limbs,
and cherished in her lap the goddess lifts him to the high
groves of Idalia, where soft marjoram him
with flowers and sweet breathing shade enfolds.
sentences.i: But Venus sheds a quiet sleep through the limbs of Ascanius, and, holding him warm in her lap, bears him up to the high groves of Idalia, where soft marjoram enfolds him in flowers and the sweet breath of its shade.
sentences.n: 'Ascanio… per membra' — 'Ascanio' is a dative of interest or possession, with 'per membra' meaning 'through his limbs'. 'inrigat' — 'irrigates', 'pours over' (like water or dew); Venus gives sleep as though by watering. 'fotum' — perfect passive participle of 'foveo', 'warmed', 'cherished', in a motherly act; 'gremio' — ablative of place. 'Idaliae' — genitive singular of the place name Idalia; Greenough's text reads 'Idaliae lucos' 'the groves of Idalia'. 'amaracus' — marjoram, a fragrant plant (Greek word for it). 'floribus et dulci adspirans… umbra' — 'adspirans' ('breathing on') agrees with 'amaracus'; 'floribus' and 'umbra' are ablatives of means with 'complectitur': it enfolds him with flowers and with its sweet-breathing shade.

sentences.t:
Iamque ibat dicto parens et dona Cupido
regia portabat Tyriis, duce laetus Achate.
sentences.l:
And now was going, obedient to the word, and gifts, Cupid,
royal ones, was bringing to the Tyrians, glad with Achates as guide.
sentences.i: And now Cupid was on his way, obedient to the order, carrying the royal gifts to the Tyrians, happy to have Achates as his guide.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'dicto parens' — 'parens' looks like the noun 'parent', but here it is the participle of 'pareo', 'obeying', and 'dicto' is its dative. 'ibat' and 'portabat' — imperfects for the continuing action (and so the stage is set for the arrival at 697). 'Tyriis' — dative of the persons to whom: the gifts are carried 'to the Tyrians', i.e. to Dido and her court. 'duce… Achate' — ablative absolute, literally 'Achates (being) leader'; Achates is Aeneas's faithful companion and was sent to the ships for Ascanius (656).

sentences.t:
Cum venit, aulaeis iam se regina superbis
aurea composuit sponda mediamque locavit.
sentences.l:
When he comes, now among the proud hangings the queen herself
on a golden couch has placed, and has set herself in the middle.
sentences.i: By the time he arrives, the queen has taken her place on a golden couch beneath splendid tapestries, in the central seat.
sentences.n: 'Cum venit' — 'when he comes': 'cum' with the indicative present (historic present), 'venit' for the arrival. 'iam' — 'already'. 'aulaeis… superbis' — ablative of place or attendant circumstance, 'among proud hangings'; the 'aulaea' were embroidered curtains or canopies. 'aurea… sponda' — ablative of place; the 'sponda' is the frame or bed of a banqueting couch. 'se composuit… mediamque locavit' — the reflexive 'se' is understood with 'locavit': 'placed (herself) in the middle'. Ancient diners reclined on couches; the central position was the place of honour.

sentences.t:
Iam pater Aeneas et iam Troiana iuventus
conveniunt, stratoque super discumbitur ostro.
sentences.l:
Now father Aeneas and now the Trojan youth
come together, and on the spread purple they recline.
sentences.i: Now father Aeneas and now the Trojan young men come in, and they take their places on couches spread with purple.
sentences.n: 'iam… et iam' — 'now… and now', as each group takes its place. 'pater Aeneas' — the title 'pater' marks him as leader. 'stratoque super discumbitur ostro' — an impersonal passive, 'it is reclined' (i.e. 'they recline'), with 'super' placed between the participle and its noun; 'ostro' is the purple cloth (Tyrian dye) spread over the couches. 'strato' is a perfect passive participle, 'spread'. Look for the impersonal passive.

sentences.t:
Dant famuli manibus lymphas, Cereremque canistris
expediunt, tonsisque ferunt mantelia villis.
sentences.l:
Servants give water to hands, and bread from baskets
they bring out, and napkins they bring, with the nap shorn.
sentences.i: Servants pour water over their hands and bring out bread from baskets, and carry towels of closely shorn wool.
sentences.n: 'lymphas' — a poetic word for 'water'. 'Cereremque' — 'Ceres' stands for 'bread' or 'grain' by metonymy (name of the goddess for what she gives); 'canistris' — ablative of place from which ('out of baskets'); 'expediunt' — 'bring out', 'set forth'. 'tonsis… villis' — ablative of description: napkins (mantelia) 'with shorn nap'. A hospitable meal in the Homeric manner: the hand-washing and the bread echo the welcome of a guest in Odyssey 1.

sentences.t:
Quinquaginta intus famulae, quibus ordine longam
cura penum struere, et flammis adolere Penatis;
sentences.l:
Fifty maids within, for whom in order the long
care it is to arrange the store, and with flames to honour the Penates;
sentences.i: Within are fifty maidservants, whose business is to lay out the long store of food in order and to feed the household gods with fire;
sentences.n: 'Quinquaginta intus famulae, quibus… cura' — dative of possession ('to whom (is) care'); the verb 'est' is dropped. 'struere' and 'adolere' — infinitives explaining the 'cura'. 'penum' — 'the store of provisions'. 'adolere' — 'to burn (in honour)', used of offerings burnt on an altar. 'Penatis' — accusative plural in -is, for 'Penates'; the household gods of the hearth and the store-room, who share in every meal (here, by a burnt offering). The model for the fifty maids is Alcinous's palace in Odyssey 7, which also has fifty serving women.

sentences.t:
centum aliae totidemque pares aetate ministri,
qui dapibus mensas onerent et pocula ponant.
sentences.l:
a hundred other maids and as many men of equal age,
who may load the tables with dishes and set out the cups.
sentences.i: a hundred more, and as many male servants of the same age, to load the tables with food and set the cups in place.
sentences.n: 'centum aliae totidemque pares aetate ministri' — 'ministri' is masculine, so 'aliae' (feminine) and 'ministri' mark a hundred women and as many men. 'pares aetate' — 'equal in age', ablative of respect. 'qui… onerent et ponant' — a relative clause of purpose, subjunctive.

sentences.t:
Nec non et Tyrii per limina laeta frequentes
convenere, toris iussi discumbere pictis.
sentences.l:
Nor less the Tyrians through the happy thresholds in crowds
assembled, bidden to recline on the embroidered couches.
sentences.i: The Tyrians too come crowding through the festive doorways, and are bidden to take their places on the embroidered couches.
sentences.n: 'Nec non et' — 'and also', a Virgilian formula (literally 'nor not and'); you will see it again and again. 'convenere' — the ending -ere for -erunt (a perfect). 'limina laeta' — 'happy thresholds', the doors of a house in festival. 'frequentes' — 'in crowds', 'in great numbers' (predicative adjective). 'toris iussi discumbere pictis' — 'iussi' + infinitive, 'ordered to recline'; 'toris… pictis' — 'on the embroidered couches' (after 'discumbere' the case may be taken as dative or as ablative of place; 'pictis' is 'painted', 'embroidered').

sentences.t:
Mirantur dona Aeneae, mirantur Iulum
flagrantisque dei voltus simulataque verba,
sentences.l:
They marvel at the gifts of Aeneas, they marvel at Iulus,
and the glowing god's features and the feigned words,
sentences.i: They marvel at the gifts of Aeneas, they marvel at Iulus, at the god's glowing face and his counterfeit speech,
sentences.n: 'Mirantur… mirantur' — the repetition (anaphora) of the verb. 'Aeneae' — genitive: gifts 'of Aeneas'. 'flagrantis… dei' — genitive singular of 'flagrans', 'blazing', 'glowing', with the god (Cupid) — the god's face blazes through the boy's disguise. 'simulataque verba' — 'feigned words', the false voice that is part of his disguise. The sentence continues into 711, which is bracketed in the edition.

sentences.t: [pallamque et pictum croceo velamen acantho.]
sentences.l: [and the robe and the veil embroidered with saffron acanthus.]
sentences.i: [and the robe, and the veil worked with saffron acanthus.]
sentences.n: Greenough prints this line inside brackets because he judges it spurious (not Virgil's); the archive keeps it, as the conventions require. It repeats, almost word for word, part of 648–649 ('pallam… et circumtextum croceo velamen acantho'), where Aeneas's gifts are first described, and that is why editors have suspected it of being a later addition. It stands here in its own unit so that the reader can see it apart. 'palla' — a woman's long robe; 'velamen' — veil; 'pictum' — 'embroidered' (painted with the needle); 'acantho' — ablative of 'acanthus', the leaf pattern.

sentences.t:
Praecipue infelix, pesti devota futurae,
expleri mentem nequit ardescitque tuendo
Phoenissa, et pariter puero donisque movetur.
sentences.l:
Above all the unhappy one, vowed to coming ruin,
cannot be filled in mind, and grows hot with gazing,
the Phoenician, and is moved alike by the boy and by the gifts.
sentences.i: Above all the unhappy Phoenician woman, marked out for the ruin that is coming, cannot satisfy her heart with looking, and burns as she gazes, stirred equally by the boy and the gifts.
sentences.n: 'Praecipue infelix' — the epithet 'infelix' is pinned to Dido again and again in the poem (749, and later); here it is joined to 'pesti devota futurae' — 'devoted (given over) to a coming doom': 'devota' agrees with Dido, and 'pesti futurae' is a dative (the i-stem dative, with 'futurae' agreeing). 'expleri mentem nequit' — 'expleri' is a passive infinitive used in the middle sense, 'to be filled (satisfied)', with 'mentem' an accusative of respect. 'ardescit tuendo' — 'grows hot by gazing': an ablative of the gerund, in the fire image. 'Phoenissa' again the subject, placed late for emphasis. 'pariter' — 'equally'.

sentences.t:
Ille ubi complexu Aeneae colloque pependit
et magnum falsi implevit genitoris amorem,
sentences.l:
He, when on Aeneas's embrace and neck he had hung
and had filled the great love of his false father,
sentences.i: When he had hung in Aeneas's embrace, about his neck, and had satisfied the great love of the father who was not his own,
sentences.n: 'Ille ubi' — 'when he (Cupid)'; the main verb 'petit' is at 717. 'pependit' — perfect of 'pendeo', 'hang'. 'complexu… collo' — ablatives, 'in the embrace and on the neck'. 'falsi genitoris' — 'his false father', because Aeneas thinks Cupid is his own son. 'implevit… amorem' — 'filled' (satisfied) the love: an ironic touch, since the love is Aeneas's for a boy who is not there.

sentences.t:
reginam petit haec oculis, haec pectore toto
haeret et interdum gremio fovet,
sentences.l:
he seeks the queen; she with her eyes, she with her whole breast
clings, and sometimes in her lap she cherishes him,
sentences.i: he goes to the queen; she clings to him with her eyes, she with her whole heart, and now and then warms him in her lap,
sentences.n: 'haec… haec' — 'she… she': the double 'haec' is Dido, the subject of 'haeret', picking up 'reginam' and emphasising her total absorption ('oculis' and 'pectore toto', ablatives of means). 'interdum' — 'now and then'. 'gremio fovet' — 'cherishes in her lap', echoing Venus's 'gremio' (692, 685).

sentences.t:
inscia Dido,
insidat quantus miserae deus;
sentences.l:
unaware, Dido, how great a god
settles on the wretched one;
sentences.i: all unaware, poor Dido, how great a god is settling upon her;
sentences.n: 'inscia Dido' — 'unaware Dido', the nominative with 'insidat' in the indirect question. 'quantus… deus' — 'how great a god', an indirect exclamation or question with the subjunctive 'insidat' ('sits down upon', hints at 'insidiae', 'ambush'). 'miserae' — dative: 'poor' Dido spoken of in third person with pity.

sentences.t:
at memor ille
matris Acidaliae paulatim abolere Sychaeum
incipit, et vivo temptat praevertere amore
iam pridem resides animos desuetaque corda.
sentences.l:
but he, mindful
of his Acidalian mother, little by little to wipe out Sychaeus
begins, and with a living love tries to forestall
her long since idle spirits and hearts unused.
sentences.i: but he, remembering his Acidalian mother, begins bit by bit to wipe out Sychaeus and to take possession, with a love that lives, of a mind long idle and a heart that has lost the habit.
sentences.n: 'at memor ille matris Acidaliae' — 'memor' takes the genitive, 'mindful of his mother'. 'Acidalia' is a title of Venus, said (by the ancient commentators) to come from a spring in Boeotia, the Acidalian spring, sacred to her and the Graces. 'Sychaeum' — Dido's husband, murdered by her brother Pygmalion, whose memory she has remained faithful to; his story is told at 343–352. 'paulatim abolere… incipit' — 'begins to efface'. 'vivo… amore' — 'with a living love', a contrast with the dead man. 'praevertere' — 'to pre-empt', 'to take possession of in advance', governing 'animos' and 'corda'. 'resides animos' and 'desueta corda' — 'idle spirits' and 'hearts out of the habit', plurals for one person (poetic plural). This sets up what happens in Book IV.

sentences.t:
Postquam prima quies epulis, mensaeque remotae,
crateras magnos statuunt et vina coronant.
sentences.l:
After the first quiet at the feast, and the tables taken away,
they set up great mixing-bowls and crown the wines.
sentences.i: When the first lull in the feasting has come, and the tables have been cleared, they set up big mixing-bowls and wreathe the wine.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Postquam' normally takes a perfect indicative; here the verbs are left out of both clauses ('prima quies epulis (fuit)' — 'the first quiet from the feast'; 'mensae remotae (sunt)'), the clipped style of a scene being set. The tables are cleared before the drinking begins. 'crateras' — Greek accusative plural; the 'crater' is the large bowl in which wine and water were mixed. 'vina coronant' — they 'crown' the wine, probably meaning they garland the bowls (or fill them to the brim, as Homer's formula for the young men who 'crowned the mixing-bowls with drink' has been understood, which Virgil may be echoing; the Latin does not settle which).

sentences.t:
Fit strepitus tectis, vocemque per ampla volutant
atria;
sentences.l:
There is a din in the halls, and their voice through the broad
halls they roll;
sentences.i: A din rises in the halls, and they send their voices rolling through the broad courts;
sentences.n: 'Fit strepitus' — 'fit' is the present of 'fio' (to become, to happen): 'a noise comes about'. 'tectis' — dative or ablative of place. 'vocem… volutant' — 'roll (their) voice' (singular for plural 'voices'); 'ampla atria' separated by the line break: the 'atrium' is the main hall.

sentences.t:
dependent lychni laquearibus aureis
incensi, et noctem flammis funalia vincunt.
sentences.l:
lamps hang down from the golden panelled ceilings,
lit, and the torches conquer night with flames.
sentences.i: lighted lamps hang from the golden panelled ceilings, and the torches overcome the night with their flames.
sentences.n: 'dependent' — 'hang down'. 'lychni' — Greek word for lamps. 'laquearibus aureis' — the 'laquearia' are panelled ceilings, often gilded, in which the sunk panels were coffered. 'incensi' — perfect passive participle, 'lit'. 'noctem flammis funalia vincunt' — 'funalia' are torches made of waxed rope; the line is framed by 'noctem' at the start and 'vincunt' at the end, with 'flammis funalia' between. Note the fire motif again.

sentences.i: Then the queen asked for a goblet heavy with jewels and gold, and filled it with pure wine, the cup that Belus and all his line had been accustomed to use;
sentences.n: 'Hic' — adverb, 'at this point' (not 'this'). 'gravem gemmis auroque' — 'heavy with gems and gold': ablatives of respect or means. 'poposcit' — perfect of 'posco'. 'mero' — 'merum' is unmixed wine, ablative of means. 'quam Belus et omnes a Belo soliti' — 'which Belus and all (descended) from Belus were accustomed (to use)': the verb is understood, and 'soliti' is the perfect participle of the semi-deponent 'soleo', with 'sunt' understood and the infinitive ('to fill', 'to use') left out. Belus is an ancestor of the Tyrian royal house. Dido's cup is a family heirloom.

sentences.t: tum facta silentia tectis:
sentences.l: then silence was made in the halls:
sentences.i: then silence fell over the halls:
sentences.n: 'tum facta silentia tectis' — 'facta' (supply 'sunt'), 'silentia' neuter plural: 'the silences were made', a poetic plural. The colon opens Dido's prayer, which is the central moment of the banquet.

sentences.t:
“Iuppiter, hospitibus nam te dare iura loquuntur,
hunc laetum Tyriisque diem Troiaque profectis
esse velis, nostrosque huius meminisse minores.
sentences.l:
“Jupiter, for to guests they say you give laws,
this day, joyful for Tyrians and for those who have set out from Troy,
may you will to be, and our descendants to remember this.
sentences.i: “Jupiter—for they say you are the giver of laws to guests—may you will this day to be a happy one for the Tyrians and for those who have come from Troy, and may our descendants remember it.
sentences.n: Dido's prayer (731–735); the mark opens it. 'Iuppiter' — as Jupiter Hospitalis (Greek Zeus Xenios), he is the god of guests and hospitality: 'hospitibus… dare iura' — 'to give laws to guests'. 'nam' is placed second, in its clause, not first: 'for, they say…'. 'velis' — an optative subjunctive, 'may you will': 'hunc… diem… esse velis'. 'Troiaque profectis' — 'Troia' without a preposition is the ablative of origin ('departed from Troy'), with 'Tyriisque' beside it a neat pairing. 'huius' — of this day. 'nostros… minores' — 'our descendants' ('minores' = those younger, those who come after).

sentences.t:
Adsit laetitiae Bacchus dator, et bona Iuno;
et vos, O, coetum, Tyrii, celebrate faventes.”
sentences.l:
May Bacchus, giver of joy, be present, and kindly Juno;
and you, O, the gathering, Tyrians, celebrate, favouring.”
sentences.i: Let Bacchus who gives gladness be with us, and kind Juno; and you, Tyrians, keep this gathering with your goodwill.”
sentences.n: 'Adsit' — optative subjunctive, 'may he be present' (the formula of invocation). 'laetitiae dator' — 'giver of joy', Bacchus. 'bona Iuno' — Juno as the goddess of marriage and of Carthage: Dido invokes her without knowing the part she has already played; the audience knows what Juno wants. 'faventes' — from 'faveo', 'favouring', with 'celebrate': in ritual 'favete linguis' means 'keep an auspicious silence', so the word carries sacral colouring. The closing mark ends Dido's prayer.

sentences.i: She spoke, and poured a libation of wine on the table, and, when it was poured, was the first to touch the cup to the rim of her lips; then she handed it to Bitias, rallying him;
sentences.n: 'Dixit' — the perfect that closes a speech. 'laticum… honorem' — 'the honour of liquids', i.e. a libation, an offering of wine to the gods; 'laticum' is a genitive plural. 'libato' — impersonal ablative absolute, 'the libation having been made'. 'summo tenus ore' — 'tenus' follows its ablative, 'as far as the edge of the mouth': she sipped only at the rim. 'increpitans' — 'chiding' in a friendly way, 'urging him on' to drink. Bitias is a Carthaginian noble.

sentences.t:
ille impiger hausit
spumantem pateram, et pleno se proluit auro
post alii proceres.
sentences.l:
he eagerly drank the foaming cup,
and in the full gold drenched himself,
after him other nobles.
sentences.i: He drank the foaming cup with a will and drenched himself in the brimming gold; then the other lords followed.
sentences.n: 'ille impiger' — 'he, not slow'. 'hausit' — 'drained', 'drew up'. 'spumantem pateram' — the cup 'foaming' with the wine. 'pleno se proluit auro' — 'drenched himself with the full gold', the gold standing for the golden cup. Greenough prints no stop after 'auro' and the sentence runs on to 'post alii proceres' (supply 'hauserunt'): the verb has to be understood from 'hausit'.

sentences.t:
Cithara crinitus Iopas
personat aurata, docuit quem maximus Atlas.
sentences.l:
With the lyre long-haired Iopas
resounds, gilded, whom greatest Atlas taught.
sentences.i: Long-haired Iopas fills the hall with the ring of his gilded lyre, the minstrel whom mighty Atlas taught.
sentences.n: 'Cithara… aurata' — ablative of means, 'with the gilded lyre' ('aurata' agrees with 'cithara'); the lyre is Greek 'kithara'. 'personat' — 'resounds', 'makes ring', with no object here: the hall rings with it. 'crinitus' — 'long-haired', the mark of the bard (Apollo is 'crinitus' too). Iopas is the court singer, a figure not otherwise known from earlier legend. 'docuit quem maximus Atlas' — Atlas, the Titan who holds up the sky, was in legend an astronomer and teacher of the stars; so Iopas's song, which follows, is a song of nature and the heavens. His song takes the place of the bards' songs at the feasts of the Odyssey.

sentences.t: Hic canit errantem lunam solisque labores;
sentences.l: Here he sings the wandering moon and the sun's toils;
sentences.i: Here he sings of the wandering moon and the labours of the sun;
sentences.n: 'errantem lunam' — 'wandering moon'; the moon and planets 'wander' in Roman astronomy. 'solis labores' — the 'toils' of the sun are its eclipses (the sun in labour), a common poetic term. Iopas's song is a list of subjects of natural philosophy in the manner of Lucretius, whom Virgil admired. Each item is a separate object of 'canit'.

sentences.t: unde hominum genus et pecudes;
sentences.l: whence the race of men and the flocks;
sentences.i: whence came the human race and the cattle;
sentences.n: 'unde' — 'whence', introducing the next item in the song. 'hominum' — genitive plural (here the regular -um). 'pecudes' — 'cattle', 'flocks', 'beasts'. The verb 'canit' of 742 governs everything to 746; the semicolons mark each subject.

sentences.t: unde imber et ignes;
sentences.l: whence rain and fires;
sentences.i: and where rain and lightning come from;
sentences.n: 'imber et ignes' — 'rain and fires' — the 'ignes' are lightning and meteors. The questions are those of the Epicurean tradition (Lucretius), the origin of the sublunar phenomena.

sentences.t: Arcturum pluviasque Hyadas geminosque Triones;
sentences.l: Arcturus, the rainy Hyades, and the twin Triones;
sentences.i: Arcturus, the rainy Hyades, and the twin Bears;
sentences.n: All accusatives after 'canit'. 'Arcturum' — a bright star (the Bear-ward), whose rising meant storms. 'pluvias Hyadas' — 'the rainy Hyades', a star-cluster in Taurus (the Greeks linked the name with 'hyein', 'to rain'). 'geminos Triones' — 'Triones' = 'plough-oxen', the seven stars of the Bear (Septentriones); 'twin' as the Great and Little Bear. Greenough's 'Triones' for the common 'Septemtriones'.

sentences.t:
quid tantum Oceano properent se tinguere soles
hiberni, vel quae tardis mora noctibus obstet.
sentences.l:
why so greatly in Ocean they hasten to dip themselves, the suns
of winter, or what delay stands in the way of the slow nights.
sentences.i: why the suns of winter are in such haste to plunge into Ocean, and what holds back the slow nights.
sentences.n: 'quid tantum' — 'why so greatly' ('quid' is an adverbial accusative, 'why'; 'tantum' 'so much'). 'properent… obstet' — subjunctives in indirect question depending on 'canit' ('he sings why…, what…'). 'se tinguere' — 'to dip themselves'; 'Oceano' — ablative of place: the great river Ocean that was thought to ring the world, into which the sun sets. 'soles hiberni' — plural 'suns' for the sun of successive days: winter days are short and winter nights long ('tardis noctibus', since they seem to drag). 'vel' — 'or'.

sentences.t: Ingeminant plausu Tyrii, Troesque sequuntur.
sentences.l: The Tyrians redouble with applause, and the Trojans follow.
sentences.i: The Tyrians applaud again and again, and the Trojans join them.
sentences.n: 'Ingeminant plausu' — 'redouble with clapping'. 'Troes' — 'Trojans', the Greek form of the nominative plural (the Latin would be 'Troiani'). 'sequuntur' — 'follow', i.e. follow suit.

sentences.i: And unlucky Dido, too, kept drawing out the night in talk of every kind, and took in a long, slow draught of love, asking much about Priam and much about Hector;
sentences.n: 'Nec non et' — again. 'trahebat' and 'bibebat' — imperfects, 'she kept on drawing out… drinking'. 'longum… amorem' — 'long (deep) draughts of love' — drinking as a figure of love, the banquet's own wine image taken further. 'super Priamo… super Hectore' — 'super' with the ablative = 'concerning' (colloquial for 'de'). 'rogitans' — frequentative of 'rogo', 'asking again and again'. The repeated 'multa… multa' frames the two names.

sentences.t:
nunc quibus Aurorae venisset filius armis,
nunc quales Diomedis equi, nunc quantus Achilles.
sentences.l:
now in what arms the son of Dawn had come,
now what sort Diomede's horses, now how great Achilles.
sentences.i: now in what armour the son of Dawn had come, now what Diomedes's horses were like, now how great Achilles was.
sentences.n: Indirect questions, with 'quibus… venisset' in the pluperfect subjunctive and the other two verbless (supply 'essent' and 'esset'). 'Aurorae… filius' — Memnon, the Ethiopian king whom Dawn bore to Tithonus; he came to help Troy and was killed by Achilles (the story of the lost epic Aethiopis). 'Diomedis equi' — usually taken as the horses Diomedes won from Rhesus (Iliad 10), whose tents Aeneas has seen on the temple wall (469–73); the question was what the horses were like. 'nunc… nunc… nunc' — a triple anaphora, showing how her questions kept changing.

sentences.i: “No, come, tell us from the very beginning, guest, of the Greeks' treachery, and the misfortunes of your people, and your wanderings;
sentences.n: Dido's speech (753–756). Greenough prints a second opening mark before 'insidias' at the head of 754, with no closing mark before it; it is a stray mark, and the speech runs on to 756. It is kept in the Latin and the word-for-word line, and left out of the free English so that the quotation marks balance. 'Immo age' — 'nay, come': 'immo' contradicts or goes one better ('rather, come now'). 'a prima… origine' — 'from the first beginning'. 'dic… nobis' — imperative with a dative. 'inquit' — 'she says', slipped in as a parenthesis in the middle of her words. 'insidias Danaum' — 'the treachery of the Danaans' (old genitive plural -um), the wooden horse. This opens the long narrative of Books II–III, as Alcinous's request to Odysseus opens the tale of Odysseus's wanderings in the Odyssey.

sentences.t:
nam te iam septima portat
omnibus errantem terris et fluctibus aestas.”
sentences.l:
for now the seventh summer carries you
wandering over all lands and waves.”
sentences.i: for this is already the seventh summer that carries you, wandering, over every land and sea.”
sentences.n: 'nam te iam septima portat… aestas' — 'for now the seventh summer carries you': the Trojans have been away from Troy for seven summers (by the count of the poem). 'errantem' — participle agreeing with 'te'. 'omnibus… terris et fluctibus' — ablatives of place, 'over all lands and waves'. The closing mark ends Dido's speech and the part.
